A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AANet study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and can be matched reliably, including material renumbered or relocated in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original screening experiments on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, pocket identification on COACH420, component ablations and additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds DEKOIS evaluation, homology-filtered training comparisons, ligand-based comparisons and quantitative pocket-coverage analysis.

M1.justification: The tri-modal alignment, cavity negatives, enlarged pockets and cross-attention aggregation remain unchanged in Sections 3.3–3.4 and Algorithms 1–3. Newly documented activity-pair masking and atom downsampling provide implementation details without establishing a revision to the original procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds screening evaluation on 77 DEKOIS targets under holo, predicted-apo annotated and predicted-apo blind conditions (Appendix C.4, Table S10). This substantially extends the evaluated protein–compound data beyond the retained benchmarks; v1 mentioned DEKOIS only in baseline training exclusions.

E2.justification: V2 adds ECFP4 to the ligand-based comparison with AANet (Table S12), and GOLD appears as an additional docking comparator in Table S10. USR and PhaseShape were already evaluated in v1 Table S1. The main screening and pocket-identification comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.5 introduces a separate control excluding training proteins containing chains with at least 90% sequence identity to DUD-E targets, using MMseqs2 on PDBbind and ChEMBL. DEKOIS evaluation additionally reports EF0.5%, while the runtime comparison distinguishes 2.8M, 10M and 100M scoring workloads. These extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original main-table protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantial generalization check through homology removal (Table S11), runtime comparisons across workloads (Table S7), and quantitative coverage and atom-count analysis supporting the 10 Å radius (Appendix D.1). The original component ablations, detector-transfer tests, t-SNE analysis and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1 newly reports pocket atom counts using mean-plus/minus summaries, including 612.68 ± 240.75 and 199.32 ± 55.04, although the dispersion measure is unspecified. Both versions retain random seed 1 in Table S4; v2 does not add repeated-run uncertainty for screening performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for DEKOIS, homology filtering, ligand-based screening, runtime and pocket coverage. DEKOIS predicted-apo blind EF0.5% is 13.33 for AANet versus 0.92 for DrugCLIP. Under the same stated settings, Table 1 also revises Glide's DUD-E holo EF1% from 18.07 to 17.25 and TankBind's LIT-PCBA experimental-apo blind EF1% from 1.97 to 3.42; corresponding AUROC entries change too. AANet's original headline scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The pocket and IoU definitions, alignment and aggregation equations, and appendix metric formulas are retained. No theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is added or revised; the new appendix discussion motivates existing design choices.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about pocket-localization failures, alignment and aggregation, and near-holo screening under structural uncertainty. The headline EF1% comparison of 11.75 versus 37.19 is unchanged; additional experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands qualifications and interpretation: structure-ID filtering may leave target redundancy, ECFP4 performance may exploit DUD-E topology bias, and larger pockets trade coverage against downsampling and irrelevant regions. Appendix D.3 explicitly acknowledges difficulties with flexible or disordered proteins and distinguishes pocket localization from full flexible-binding modeling.

D1.justification: V2 announces public implementation access and supplies an AANet code link absent from v1. New Appendix B.2 specifies ChEMBL molecule and activity filters, target mapping and masking of known positive pairs using UniProt IDs and InChI keys. Appendix D.1 also specifies uniform downsampling to at most 256 atoms, materially improving documentation of the existing pipeline.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to FlowDock, MMseqs2 and extended-connectivity fingerprints, and discusses PoseBusters when motivating physical plausibility. The ligand-based comparison broadens contextual positioning, but the main related-work narrative and novelty claims remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order remain intact. V2 inserts ChEMBL-processing documentation, expands Appendix C, adds an Appendix D discussion, improves specific appendix references, and updates affiliations, acknowledgements and the conference footer. These are localized structural and editorial changes rather than a broad rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the appendix's tabular presentation with dedicated runtime, DEKOIS, homology-filtering and ligand-based comparison tables. Figure 3 is redrawn with revised phase labels and clearer training-data flow. Existing AUROC and full-holo tables are retained as Tables S8 and S9; Table S12 partly redisplays earlier USR and PhaseShape results alongside the new comparison.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens validation by addressing the target-redundancy concern left open by v1's structure-ID filtering: AANet retains its advantage under the added 90% sequence-identity exclusion control. DEKOIS evaluation and the ECFP4 comparison broaden scrutiny of generalization and benchmark bias. Detailed ChEMBL processing, implementation-access information and explicit flexible-protein limitations also improve reproducibility and scope. Screening uncertainty across training runs remains unreported, but the combined gains substantially improve the paper's evidential foundation.
